title: BPMN 2.0.2 documentation guidelines for process and collaboration generation
purpose: Operational paraphrases for an LLM that generates BPMN 2.0 XML from a process description.

normative_source.title: Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN), Version 2.0.2

profile_scope: Tasks, subprocesses, events, gateways and sequence flows
Common data objects and documentation artifacts
outside_prompt_scope: Vendor extensions and engine-specific deployment attributes
methodology_note: Concise paraphrases, not copied normative text. This common generation profile does not replace XSD validation or the full OMG specification.

rules.instruction: Return one complete, well-formed bpmn:definitions document and no surrounding explanation or Markdown fence.
Declare the BPMN model namespace http://www.omg.org/spec/BPMN/20100524/MODEL and a non-empty targetNamespace on bpmn:definitions.

Assign a unique XML id to every referenced element. Resolve all Ref attributes to existing, type-compatible elements. For example, a split gateway and the gateway that joins its branches get two different ids, such as Gateway_Approval_Split and Gateway_Approval_Join.
rules.pilot_note: example added in v2.2 after the pilot (2 duplicate gateway ids)

rules.instruction: Escape XML special characters in names, documentation and expressions. Do not emit undeclared prefixes, duplicate attributes or unclosed tags.
Do not add BPMN-DI, vendor extensions or execution-engine attributes unless the requested output explicitly requires them.

Follow the BPMN XML schema: never put a documentation element directly inside bpmn:definitions, and never nest a sequenceFlow inside a task, gateway or event. If you add an ioSpecification, it must contain its dataInput and dataOutput elements first, then at least one inputSet and one outputSet, even if empty: <bpmn:inputSet/><bpmn:outputSet/>.
Write default, sourceRef, targetRef, attachedToRef, processRef and messageRef as attributes, never as child elements, and give every association both a sourceRef and a targetRef.
Model every distinct activity, event, participant, decision, branch, loop, message and outcome stated in the description. Do not invent process facts.
Do not merge separately described actions into one task or split one stated action without a process reason. Preserve described dependencies.
Use short, faithful labels in the input language. Prefer verb-object activity names and meaningful business triggers or outcomes for events.
When the description does not justify a specialized construct, use the simplest compatible BPMN construct and do not guess missing semantics.
Represent each modeled internal workflow with bpmn:process. Use isExecutable=false unless execution-ready behavior is explicitly required and fully specified.
Keep each flow node and sequence flow inside its owning process or subprocess. Sequence flows never cross pool or subprocess boundaries.
Build a connected path from each modeled start to an end or intentionally continuing state. Avoid accidental disconnected flow nodes.
Allow multiple start or end events when the description has distinct triggers or outcomes. Do not force all outcomes into one end.

Give every process and every expanded subProcess its own explicit start event and end event. A trigger that occurs after the main flow (for example later feedback or a return) is joined to the main flow by a gateway, or modeled as an event subprocess or a separate process.
rules.source_clause: 10.2, 10.3.5; stricter than BPMN, which allows implicit start and end events in some cases

rules.instruction: Use bpmn:task for atomic work when the execution mode is unspecified. A task contains no internal flow.
Use bpmn:userTask for human work assisted by software and bpmn:manualTask for human work performed without an execution application.
Use bpmn:serviceTask for automated service work, bpmn:scriptTask for an explicit script, and bpmn:businessRuleTask for explicit rule evaluation.
Use bpmn:sendTask or bpmn:receiveTask when sending or waiting for a message is itself the modeled unit of work.
Distinguish message tasks from message events: a task models performed work; an event models a message occurrence affecting flow.
Model performer information only when responsibility is stated. Prefer lanes for ordinary organizational responsibility.
Several unconditional outgoing flows from one activity can all proceed. Use a gateway when the description requires a decision or synchronization.
Do not infer a task subtype only from a verb in its label; require supporting meaning in the full description.
Use bpmn:subProcess for a nested workflow belonging to its parent process; keep all internal nodes and flows inside it.
Use bpmn:callActivity only to invoke a separately defined reusable process or global task; make calledElement resolvable in the intended model context.
An ordinary embedded subprocess participates in normal sequence flow and may contain its own starts, ends, activities, gateways and flows.
For an event subprocess set triggeredByEvent=true, use exactly one triggered start event, and add no incoming or outgoing sequence flow.
Use standard loop or multi-instance characteristics only when repetition is explicit; choose sequential or parallel instances from the description.
Use transaction, ad-hoc or compensation behavior only when its specific semantics are explicitly described.
Inside an ordinary subProcess (embedded or called), use only a None start event; typed start triggers are reserved for top-level processes and event subprocesses.
Use start events for stated process triggers. A start event has no incoming sequence flow and is not the source of a message flow.
Use end events for terminal outcomes. An end event has no outgoing sequence flow and is not the target of a message flow.
Use an intermediate catch event when flow waits for a trigger and an intermediate throw event when flow emits or raises a result.
Use message events for directed participant communication, signal events for broadcasts, and timer events for stated dates, durations or cycles.
Use conditional, error, escalation, cancel, compensation, link, multiple or terminate events only when their specific semantics and placement are supported.
Use a none start when no trigger is stated. Never use a none start for an event subprocess.
Attach a boundary event with attachedToRef. Set cancelActivity=true when it interrupts the activity and false only for supported non-interrupting behavior.
Use an interrupting event-subprocess start when the parent scope stops; use non-interrupting only when the parent continues.
Use a terminate end only when all remaining activity in the current scope must end immediately.
Keep catch and throw direction consistent and avoid representing one occurrence redundantly as an equivalent adjacent task and event.
Attach to an activity boundary only these triggers: message, timer, escalation, conditional, signal, error, cancel, compensation or multiple. Never a none or link event.
An error boundary event is always interrupting (cancelActivity=true); a cancel boundary event is used only on a transaction subProcess.

Respect event positions: a none intermediate event is catch-only in normal flow and never on a boundary; link events are intermediate-only, thrown and caught in pairs at the same process level, and a catching link has no incoming sequence flow; terminate is an end event only.
For a message event, put messageRef on its bpmn:messageEventDefinition, never on the event element itself.
Use gateways to control divergence and convergence, never to represent work. Identify exclusive, inclusive, parallel, event-driven or complex behavior.
Use an exclusive split when exactly one data-based alternative runs. Add supported conditions and at most one default fallback.
Use an exclusive merge for alternative paths; it does not wait for inactive alternatives.
Use a parallel split when all outgoing branches start. Do not add decision conditions to parallel branches.
Use a parallel join when a shared continuation waits for all active parallel branches. Never use it to join mutually exclusive alternatives.
Use an inclusive split when one or more conditions can be true; use an inclusive join to synchronize only activated reachable branches.
Use an event-based gateway when the first occurring event selects the path. Target supported catching events or receive tasks, not ordinary tasks.
Use a complex gateway only for an explicitly described rule that XOR, OR and AND cannot express. Prefer separate split and join gateways for clarity.
Give the outgoing sequence flows of an event-based gateway no conditionExpression; the first occurring target event selects the path.
Every gateway either splits (two or more outgoing flows) or merges (two or more incoming flows); never give a gateway one incoming and one outgoing flow.
Use bpmn:sequenceFlow for execution order between flow nodes in the same process or subprocess scope; set valid sourceRef and targetRef values.
Only activities, gateways and events are sequence-flow endpoints. Never connect sequence flows to pools, lanes, data objects, groups or annotations.
Keep incoming and outgoing references consistent where used. Never add incoming flow to a start or outgoing flow from an end.
Use a boolean formal conditionExpression on a conditional flow only when the description supports the condition.
Reference a default flow with the source activity or gateway default attribute and give the default flow no conditionExpression.
Trace every split to continuations or endings. Add a join only when paths reunite and choose matching waiting semantics.
Represent loops only when repetition is stated and provide a meaningful exit unless endless behavior is explicit.
Create bpmn:collaboration when distinct participants interact and represent every participant as a bpmn:participant pool.
A white-box participant references its process with processRef. A black-box participant has no processRef and no modeled internal workflow.
Use sequence flows inside one participant process and message flows between different participants. Never use sequence flow across pools.
Direct each message flow from sender to receiver. Its endpoints must belong to different pools and be valid interaction nodes.
Do not attach message flows to lanes, gateways, data objects, groups or annotations; use participant boundaries or eligible flow nodes.
Create reusable bpmn:message elements and messageRef only when communication content or shared message identity matters.
Do not create separate pools for ordinary internal roles unless the description treats them as independent communicating participants.
Use lanes to partition one process by a stated role, department, system or responsibility; lanes are not separate processes.
Each lane flowNodeRef identifies a node in the owning process. Assign nodes according to stated responsibility and avoid arbitrary membership.
Sequence flows may cross lanes in one process. Use message flows across participant pools, never between lanes.
Lanes may be nested: a lane can contain a child laneSet that partitions it further; every flowNodeRef at any depth references nodes of the one owning process.
Put each flow node, including gateways and events, in exactly one lane.
Use dataObjectReference for process-instance data and dataStoreReference for persistent information available beyond one process instance.
Use data input and output associations between data and activities. Data associations do not define execution order.
Use text annotations and associations only for explanatory information; they do not control execution.
Use groups only for documentation or analysis categories; groups create no scope and change no flow behavior.
Verify XML syntax, namespaces, unique IDs, reference types, scopes, and all incoming and outgoing flow references.
Verify every start-to-end path, loop exit, branch condition and join; prevent deadlocks from incompatible branch and join semantics.
Verify processRef values, lane membership, message-flow endpoints and directions, and the prohibition on sequence flows between pools.
Compare the model with the description; remove unsupported elements and retain every explicitly stated alternative, outcome and collaboration.

When the description states that a later step is performed only if a stated condition holds, using an 'if ... then' phrasing that gates that step on a decision made earlier in the process: Model an exclusive gateway immediately before the gated step, with one outgoing branch that leads to the gated step under the stated condition and another branch that skips it or leads to the process's alternative path. Keep the gateway after the activity that establishes the condition, so the decision is evaluated in the order the description gives.

When the description names several actions within one phase in a comma-separated or 'and'-joined list, such as 'A, B, and C', or joins two actions with 'and' in one clause: Model each listed action as its own task, in the order the description states them, connected by sequence flows. Do not combine the listed actions into one task label, and do not drop any action from the list.

When the description says the process starts when a party (such as a department) performs a stated action, for example identifying a need, before any further work is described: Model a start event for the triggering occurrence, and place a separate task directly after it that is named with the action the party performs. Do not fold that action into the start event's label. Connect the task to the next step of the described flow.

When the description says that a stage begins after a preceding step is accepted, names the stage's start, and then lists several separate activities that the stage includes, with the stage ending only after those activities are finished: Model a separate task that represents starting the stage, placed directly after the preceding step, and label it with the start verb the description uses for the stage (for example 'Begin ...'). Then model each listed activity as its own task after it, labeled with the action the description gives for that activity. Do not label any listed activity with the stage-start verb, and do not let the starting task stand in for one of the listed activities.

When the description lists several activities of a stage with no order stated between them, and the stage or the process ends only after all of those activities are finished: Model a parallel gateway directly after the task that starts the stage or precedes the list. Fork it into one task per listed activity, each as its own task with the action the description gives for it. Connect every one of those tasks into a second parallel gateway that joins them. Place the join before the next step or the end event, and connect it onward from there. Do not chain the unordered activities in sequence, and do not use an exclusive gateway for either the fork or the join.

When the description offers an either-or choice between two named ways of carrying out one step (for example 'X or Y'), and both ways continue to the same following step: Model each named way as its own task or path. Place an exclusive gateway before the alternatives to split the flow, with one outgoing branch per alternative. Join the alternative branches with an exclusive gateway before the common next step. Do not drop an alternative, and do not collapse the alternatives into one generic activity.

When the description says that an activity follows the receipt of an item or delivery (for example 'upon receiving X, ...'), and it does not describe any message, signal, time or condition that the process waits for: Do not insert an intermediate catch event for the receipt. Connect the preceding activity directly by a sequence flow to the first activity the description gives after the receipt. Use an intermediate catch event only when the description states a wait for an external message, signal, timer or condition.

When the description states that two or more activities are carried out at the same time (one of them ongoing, such as monitoring, while others such as follow-up or analysis run in parallel) and a later step, such as the closing of the process, is described only after these activities are complete: Open the concurrent activities with a parallel gateway (split), so that all branches start. Close the branches with a parallel gateway (join) before the step that follows them, and connect the join to the concluding step with a sequence flow. Do not use exclusive gateways for these branches, and do not add conditions to the parallel flows.

When the description says the process ends after a participant carries out a stated activity, and it names no message, signal, timer or condition that the process waits for: Model that activity as a task in the participant's pool or lane, placed before the end event and connected by sequence flows. Do not model it as an intermediate catch event. Use an intermediate catch event only where the description states a wait for an external message, signal, time or condition.

When the description applies one action verb to several named objects joined by 'and' or 'or' within one sentence, such as 'X and Y' or 'X or Y' used as the objects of that action, so each named object is a separate thing the action is performed on: Model each named object as its own task, with the action label taken from the description and the object named separately, placed in the order the description gives. Do not merge the named objects into one combined task label, and do not drop any of them. If the sentence makes the whole group optional, place each of these tasks in the branch that the optional-step gateway controls.

When the description ends the process with a choice between alternative outcomes, each stated as an action performed on the handled object, and the outcomes do not lead back into the flow: Place an exclusive gateway after the last step that produces the choice, with one outgoing branch per stated outcome. On each branch, model the outcome's stated action as its own task on the handled object, and follow that task with its own end event. Do not connect the gateway directly to end events, and do not drop any outcome.

When the description states that the flow terminates in one of two alternative actions performed on the subject, with each action named in the description: Place an exclusive gateway at the point where the alternative is chosen. After each branch, model the named action as its own task, labeled with the action the description names, and connect that task to its own end event. Do not model an action only as an end event labeled with the resulting state, and do not merge the alternative action tasks into one task.

When the description lists two or more activities that follow one step or act on the same item, and it states no order among them, only that they are performed to be completed before a later step: Model these activities as the outgoing branches of a parallel gateway that opens them all, and close them with a parallel gateway that joins all branches before the next step that depends on their completion. Do not sequence them one after another and do not add decision conditions to these branches.

When the description says the process starts when a party performs a stated action (for example, submitting something) and names no message, signal, or other message exchange that the action sends: Model the process start as a bpmn:startEvent with no incoming sequence flow. Place a plain bpmn:task (not a bpmn:sendTask) for the party's action directly after the start event, and connect it by a sequence flow to the next step of the described flow. Do not add a second start event for the action, and do not add an end event after the action.

When the description lists several actions that all occur after one completed step, with no condition choosing among them, and a later step is reached only after all of those actions are finished: Model a parallel gateway split directly after the completed step, with one outgoing sequence flow to each listed action, and a matching parallel gateway join that collects those actions before the later step. Do not use an exclusive gateway or a condition on these branches.

When the description says the process begins when a participant performs an action (for example, filling in information or signing up) that is followed by further system activity: Model the process start as a plain start event, then model the participant's described action as a task placed after it and before the next system activity. Do not use the action as the label of the start event.

When The description names a message that a process event sends or waits for, so the model needs a message event definition.: Place the event's name on the event element itself (or on a referenced bpmn:message element). On the bpmn:messageEventDefinition, set only its id and messageRef attributes, and never give it a name attribute, because the BPMN 2.0.2 XSD does not allow one.

When the description states that a review leads to an approval decision, that only the approved outcome is then carried out, and that the approved outcome consists of several actions that must all be done before the process moves on: Model the review as a task, and the approval decision as an exclusive gateway with a conditioned approved branch and a separate non-approved branch that ends in its own end event. On the approved branch, first place a task that carries out the approval, then open a parallel gateway that splits into one task per required action, and close those tasks with a matching parallel gateway join before the next step. Do not skip the approval task or route the approved actions directly from the decision gateway.

When the description states that a decision outcome is communicated to a participant, and one outcome requires a further processing step while the other outcome only needs its own notice, with both paths then leading to a common closing step: Model each outcome as its own branch. Place an exclusive gateway after the decision has been determined, and give each outcome flow a condition that matches the description's wording. Put the outcome-specific notice task on the branch whose outcome needs it, and do not reuse one shared notice task for both outcomes. Place the further processing step after the notice for the outcome that requires it, connected by a sequence flow. Reunite the branches with an exclusive join gateway before the common closing step or end event. Do not leave a branch without a continuation.

When the description states that, after the case has been closed, an outside participant can optionally perform an action such as giving a response or input, and the description describes this as something the participant does rather than something the process waits to receive: Model this optional action as a task performed by that participant, placed in the participant's pool or lane and connected after the closing step. Do not model it as an intermediate catch event that waits for a message, and do not add a receive event that the process must wait on.

When the description says the process ends when some occurrence happens, and in the same sentence it names a participant who then begins or carries out a further action (for example, putting a decision into effect): Do not place the end event directly after the occurrence named as the end condition. Model the participant's described further action as its own task, connected by a sequence flow from that occurrence and followed by the end event. Keep the end event after that task so the action is not dropped.

When the description ends the process with a hand-off step, and then states that the recipient goes on to carry out a further action: Model that stated further action as its own task, placed after the hand-off task and before the end event, and label it with the action the description names. Do not fold this action into the end event's label, and do not let the hand-off task stand in for it.

When the description states that a review stage produces feedback, and a later exclusive choice decides whether further changes are needed in response to that feedback: Model the handling of the feedback as its own task placed after the review task and before the exclusive gateway that decides whether changes are required. Route the gateway's changes-needed branch back to the revision work and its no-changes branch onward, so the feedback is processed as a distinct step before the decision.

When the description names an activity or outcome in a short phrase, and a generated task or event label adds qualifiers such as the time period, the recipient, or a status that the description does not use as the activity's name: Label the task or event with the core verb-object action or outcome that the description names, and omit added qualifiers (periods, recipients, statuses) unless the description uses them as part of the activity's name.

When the description says the process begins when a participant performs a named action, and that same action is also described as a step the participant carries out: Model a start event that marks the beginning of the process, followed by a task that carries the named action as an activity. Do not use the start event's label as the only representation of that action, so the action appears as a task in the flow.

When the description states that a group's preparation work is completed before a separately described activity that a different party carries out, and that this party's later review of findings is a distinct step: Model the activity that the other party carries out as its own task. Place it after the join that completes the preparation work and before the task for reviewing findings, with sequence flows connecting them in that order. Do not merge this activity into the review task, and do not drop it because the review task seems to cover the same party.

When the description mentions an activity only inside a phrase that orders other steps (such as a timing reference placed before or after other steps), and that activity is itself performed between the steps it is positioned between: Model the mentioned activity as its own task. Place it in the sequence between the step that precedes it and the step that follows it, and connect them with sequence flows so the preceding stage flows into it and it flows into the following step. Do not omit it because it appears only as a timing reference, and do not merge it into the neighbouring tasks.

When the description states that a conditional branch sends a request to another party and that the process continues only after that party's response, with the response then leading on to the activity that follows the branch: When a conditional split leads to a request and a later response, model the response as an activity that receives its own incoming sequence flow from the split and sends a sequence flow onward to the merge point where the unconditional path rejoins. Join the no-issue path and the response path with a gateway before the next activity, so that no response activity forms a separate start-to-end chain.

When the description says a reviewer may either approve an item or send it back for rework, and the send-back branch is followed by a further action and then by a resubmission for another review of the same item: Place an exclusive gateway at the decision point, with one outgoing branch per outcome the description names. On the approval branch, model the approval as its own task on the item. On the send-back branch, model the return action the description names as its own task, then model the rework as a separate task, then model the resubmission as its own task that leads back to the same review step. Do not merge the return action and the rework into one task, and do not label the rework task with the name of the return action.

When the description states that, after an ordered sequence of earlier steps has finished, one further action is performed that concludes the whole process (for example 'the whole process is then wrapped up'): Model the stated concluding action as its own task placed after the last preceding step and before the final end event, labeled with the action the description gives. Do not replace it with an end event alone, and do not drop it or merge it into the label of an earlier task.

When the description states that a conditional branch starts a named activity, and the steps it involves are described as its contents rather than as steps of the main flow: Model the named activity as a single task on that conditional branch, connected by sequence flows to the surrounding gateways. Do not replace it with an embedded subprocess that has its own start and end events, and do not lift its listed contents into the main flow as separate branches unless the description sequences them as main steps.

When the description states that a participant itself receives or confirms the result of a step, and a next action follows directly after it, with no stated waiting time and no external message or condition the process waits for: Model that result as a task carried out by the participant, placed in the sequence before the next action. Use an intermediate catch event or an event-based gateway only when the description states that the process waits for an external message, signal, time or condition.

When the description names alternative outcomes of one activity, joined by 'or', where only one of the alternatives will be carried out: Model each named alternative as its own task placed after an exclusive gateway that splits the flow, and do not merge the alternatives into one task whose label lists them all.

When the description states that several activities are carried out side by side (linked by 'while', 'and', or 'in any order') and a later step may only be reached once all of them are complete: Model each of the side-by-side activities as its own task, each on a separate branch opened by a parallel split gateway. Close all branches with a parallel join gateway before the later step, so the next step waits for every branch. Do not merge the activities into one task or subprocess, do not drop any of them, and do not insert an exclusive gateway or decision condition among the branches.

When the description states that after a decision point one activity is always performed, while another activity after the same point is performed only if a condition holds, and both branches later continue to a common step: Model the split as an inclusive gateway: give the optional branch its condition and leave the always-performed branch unconditional, so both can be activated together. Rejoin the branches with a matching inclusive gateway that proceeds once the activated branches complete. Do not use an exclusive gateway for the optional branch followed by a parallel join, because a parallel join would wait for a branch that may be skipped, and an exclusive join would not synchronize the always-performed branch.

When the description bases a branch on a stated property of an item (for example its amount or size), and a generic yes/no question about whether a later activity happens would be the natural gateway label: Model the exclusive gateway for that branch and label it with the tested property in the description's own wording (for example, the property and its threshold or category, as a short condition), not with a generic question about whether a later activity occurs. Label each outgoing branch with the outcome for that property value, and label each activity with the verb and object the description uses for that action.

When the description says one participant asks several outside parties to return a response and then picks one of those responses, and gives no steps for the outside parties beyond returning their response: Model the request and the selection as tasks in the lane of the requesting participant, in the order the description states them, with a gateway only if the outcome branches. Do not create a separate pool for the outside parties and do not add message flows to or from them. Use a separate pool with message flows only when the description gives the outside parties their own steps or treats them as independent communicating participants.

When the description names a role or department that performs activities only in one or some conditional branches of the process, and does not perform any in the other branches: Model that role as its own lane inside the pool that owns the process, even though its activities occur only in some branches. Place every activity the description attributes to that role, including the activities of that role inside a branch, in its lane. Do not merge that role's activities into the lane of another role, and do not omit the lane because the role is inactive in the remaining branches.

When the description states that a branch that follows a decision ends with a named action performed on the subject of the process (for example, closing it) before the process ends: Model each such branch as its own task, labeled with the action the description names, placed after the decision branch and before that branch's end event. Do not replace the action with a bare end event, and do not drop it or merge it into the label of an earlier task.

When the description has an interactive software system, used by a person in one participant's organization, that sends a request to a process run by another participant and must receive that process's outcome back in the system: Model the software system as its own black-box pool with no internal workflow. Connect its request to a message start event in the other participant's process pool with a message flow. Connect that process's final send task back to the same software system pool with a message flow. Do not represent this exchange as a sequence flow, and do not fold the software system into a lane of the other pool or replace it with a generic person pool.

When the description says that a cycle returns the flow to an earlier point (for example, to receiving new items again), and a later stated condition either sends the flow back into that cycle or ends the process: Model the step that decides whether the cycle continues as an exclusive gateway. Give one outgoing sequence flow that returns to the merge gateway at the start of the cycle while the continuation condition holds, and one outgoing sequence flow to an end event for the stated termination outcome. Check that every merge gateway in the cycle has at least one path to an end event, and do not leave a cycle without an exit.

When the description states that a party may optionally carry out an activity between two steps, and names no message, signal, time or condition that the process waits for: Model that activity as exactly one task performed by that party, placed in the sequence where the description places it, and label it with the action verb and object the description states. Do not model it as an intermediate catch event that waits for it, and do not add a second element (such as a manual task) for the same activity.

When the description states that one step requires several concurrent activities or several parties to be handled together, and a later point is described as needing all of them finished or available: Model each concurrent activity or party as its own branch after a parallel gateway fork, with its own task or event in each branch, and close the branches with a parallel gateway join before the later point. Do not collapse the branches into one activity, do not let a single branch continue alone, and do not use an exclusive gateway for a join where every branch must complete.

When the description is long and contains several separately headed sections, each with its own rules, obligations or responsible parties, that a modeler might be tempted to write out as separate documents: Emit exactly one bpmn:definitions root for the whole description. Place every section's process, collaboration or participant elements inside that single root, and place the bpmndi:BPMNDiagram element inside it as its last item. Never open a second bpmn:definitions element, nested or appended after the diagram, and never close the root before the end of the document.

When the description states that one outcome of a decision (for example, a choice being accepted) triggers several follow-up effects that happen as soon as that outcome occurs, with no order stated among them, and these effects must all be done before the process continues: After the decision gateway for that outcome, model a parallel gateway that opens one outgoing sequence flow to each follow-up effect, with each effect as its own task or send task. Close those branches with a matching parallel gateway join before the process continues. Do not sequence the effects one after another, and do not put decision conditions on these branches.

When the description states that a participant must perform a stated action a fixed number of times, with no stated decision that depends on the count: Model the stated repeated action as an activity in the performing participant's lane or pool, placed in the described order, not as an exclusive gateway that checks how many repetitions have occurred. Add a gateway only when the description states a choice that depends on the count.

When the description says that something obtained in an earlier step is passed on to a set of performers who then process it, so the passing-on is a distinct step between obtaining it and the performers' processing: Model the passing-on as its own manual task performed by the party that passes it on. Place it after the task that obtains the object and before the performers' processing task, connected by sequence flows in that order. Do not omit the passing-on step and do not merge it into the processing task.

When the description states that a repeated activity consumes an input that can be exhausted, and that once the input is exhausted a named replenishment step must occur before the activity can proceed: Model an exclusive gateway directly after each consumption of the input by the repeated activity, with a condition asking whether the input remains. Assign the branch where input remains a condition matching that wording and route it onward to the next step. Assign the exhausted branch a condition matching the empty state and route it to the replenishment step the description names, then return the flow to the point of consumption. Do not place the check only before the first consumption, and do not leave the exhausted outcome without a continuation.

When the description says a work item is initiated (for example, requests are sent to external parties) and its result is only awaited later, possibly in parallel with other work: Model the initiating work as its own task in the flow, placed before any parallel split that runs it alongside other work. Model the later awaited result as a separate intermediate catch event that follows, and do not let the catch event replace the initiating task.

When the description names a specific recipient party (for example a named organisation, unit or place) of a request or piece of work, including inside an example, and a separate send step is made for that party: Label the send task with the recipient name exactly as the description gives it, not with a generic collective term such as 'all groups' or 'the units'. Add a labelled send task only for recipients the description actually names, and do not invent further recipients from other sources.

When the description says the process asks outside helpers to carry out physical work, and the next step follows once that work is done, but the description names no message, signal, time or condition that the process waits for: Model the helpers' physical work as a manual task placed in the sequence before the next step that depends on it. Do not model the completion of that work as an intermediate catch event, and do not add a receive event for it.

When the description says that a participant sends requests to a party outside the modeled flow, asking it to carry out work, and it names no response, notice or condition that is awaited before the flow continues: Model the sending of the requests as one send task, labeled with the sending action and its content as the description states them, and placed where the description places the sending. Model the work performed by the outside party as a separate task placed after the send task, in the sequence where the description places that work. Do not merge the sending and the work into one task, do not label the sending as a generic call or step, and do not add an intermediate catch event for a response the description does not state.

When the description lists several items that the system provides at the same time, with no stated order among them and no condition choosing between them, so all of them are delivered: Model each of these items as its own concurrent branch. Open the branches with a parallel split gateway and close them with a parallel join gateway before the shared continuation. Do not sequence the items one after another and do not place an exclusive or inclusive gateway among them.

When the description says a system provides guidance or information to an actor, and the actor then performs physical work that this guidance describes, with no system involvement in the physical work itself: Model the system's provision of the guidance as a task performed by the system (a serviceTask, or a userTask if the actor operates the system), placed before the physical work and labeled with the provision action the description states. Model the actor's hands-on work as a bpmn:manualTask performed by the actor, placed after the guidance task and labeled with the physical action the description states. Do not swap these labels, so that the physical work is not labeled as a system task and the provision of guidance is not labeled as the work itself.

When The description says a metric is computed from several measured components, each of which is obtained from an external system before the calculation step.: Model the retrieval of each component as its own bpmn:serviceTask that calls the external system, placed before the calculation task. Do not fold several component retrievals into a single receiveTask or other single task.

When the description tells of a repeated activity that resumes after an interruption, and a condition that ends the whole process while the repetition otherwise continues: Model the repeated flow with a decision point that checks the condition. Connect the branch where the condition holds to its own path that ends in an explicit end event. If the description attaches a further step to that ending, place it as a task before the end event. The repeated flow keeps its own exit, so every loop has a way out and the process has at least one explicit end event.

When the description states that a person performs a named action on a monitored device (such as restarting, repairing or disconnecting it) and the flow then continues or ends, and the description does not state that the process waits for an external message, signal, time or condition for that action: Model each such person-performed action as a manual task named after the action the person performs, on the branch where it occurs, placed before the step that continues or ends the flow. Do not model it as an intermediate catch event, a start event, or an expanded subprocess. Use an intermediate catch event or an event-based gateway only where the description states that the process waits for an external message, signal, time or condition.

When the description says that after a prior step, the process must wait for an external party to respond or arrive at a time not fixed in advance, and a later step or decision depends on that response or arrival: Model an intermediate catch event that represents the wait between the prior step and the dependent step or gateway. Do not fold the waiting into the prior task, do not model the wait as a separate task, and do not connect the two steps with a plain sequence flow that hides the wait.

When the description says that a participant itself gathers or describes information and then forwards it to another participant, with no statement that the sender waits for a reply: Model the gathering or describing of the information as a task performed by that participant (a manual or user task, according to who does the work), placed directly before a separate send task that transmits the information. Do not model that gathering step as a receive task, and do not omit it. Use a receive task only when the description states that the process waits for an incoming message.

When the description says that a visit or attempt by an outside party may end without completing the job, so that the job must wait for a further visit by that party before it can proceed: Model the attempt as a task that follows the intermediate catch event for the party's visit. Place an exclusive gateway after the attempt. Give one outgoing flow that continues to the step that depends on the completed job. Give a second outgoing flow that returns to the same intermediate catch event, so the process waits again for the party. Do not end the process at the failed attempt, and do not model the return as a plain flow back to the earlier task that skips the wait.

When the description attaches a manner or intensity adjective (for example 'enthusiastic') to an activity, describing how the work is performed rather than what is done: Label the task with the core verb and object that the description uses for the work, and leave out the manner or intensity adjectives. Keep the noun the description uses for the thing acted on, so the label names the same action the description states.

When the description states that an earlier check is restarted only for one stated outcome (for example, when a required item is not available and the next item is taken), and it also describes a step that completes an awaited delivery or event and is followed by a different named step in sequence: Model the restart flow back to the earlier check only on the branch carrying that stated outcome. The step that completes the awaited event gets a single outgoing flow to the next step the description names, with no flow back to any earlier check. Give the check task its own incoming flow from the preceding step, and insert a merge gateway before it only where the description has a real join of alternative paths.

When the description states that an exclusive decision has an alternative branch in which an actor performs a described action (for example taking an item away or declaring an activity finished), and the description does not say that this branch ends the whole process: Model the alternative branch as a task labeled with the actor and the described action, placed after the decision gateway. Route its outgoing flow into the merge gateway that joins the branches before the shared continuation, instead of giving it its own end event. Use a separate end event only for an outcome the description explicitly presents as terminal.

When the description states that a condition evaluated after an activity determines whether that activity is repeated or whether an alternative branch is taken, in which a named step is performed before the flows rejoin at a later merge point: Model the named step on the alternative branch as its own task placed after the exclusive gateway, connected to the gateway by a sequence flow labeled with its condition. Connect that task to the joining gateway. Do not connect the gateway directly to the join and do not omit the named step. Keep the repeat branch as a separate flow back to the start of the repeated activities, and do not insert a join gateway that the description does not state.

When the description says that one actor checks an output prepared by another actor and then marks it with one of two outcomes, where one outcome sends the work back for repetition and the other lets the process carry on: Model the check as its own task. Model the marking as a separate task placed before an exclusive gateway. On the repetition branch, place a task that returns the work to the earlier actor for repetition, then route back to that earlier activity. On the continuation branch, place a task that carries the process on. Do not replace either outcome with a bare flow or an end event, and do not fold the marking into the check task.

When the description states that a step is received or completed by a named role or position (a person or group identified by their job function), so the task for that step is performed by that role: Label the user or manual task for that step with the described action together with the role that performs it, using the role wording the description gives. Do not reduce the label to the bare action verb and object, since the role is part of what the description states.

When the description states that a participant performs one of two alternative actions in response to a preceding step, linked by 'or' (for example, one outcome or the other, each stated as a separate action of that participant): Model the alternatives as a diverging exclusive gateway placed after the step they respond to. Give each stated alternative its own task, with one outgoing sequence flow from the gateway to each task. Do not merge the alternatives into a single task, and do not connect them with parallel flows that would make both happen.

When the description says the process begins with a participant's sending action and states no event that triggers the process: Model a none start event as the process entry, with no incoming sequence flow, and connect it by a sequence flow to the first activity, which is the sending action. Keep the sending action as a send task that is followed by the activity that receives the sent item, so that no step lacks its incoming or outgoing flow.

When the description gives one initiating action for the process and then a sequence of steps in which each later step follows from the outcome of earlier ones (for example, continuing on success or stopping on failure), and it names no separate trigger for any other part of the process: Model one start event for the process, connected by a sequence flow to the first step of the sequence. Route every later step, including any stop outcome, from that main flow. Do not add a second start event whose path forms a separate start-to-end chain that is not joined to the main flow.

update_note: v2.2 (pilot round 2, Luna first models with v2.1: L3 failures 7 -> 3, L1 failures 4 -> 5): XML-06 gives the exact inputSet/outputSet snippet, XML-07 adds messageRef to the attribute list, and the existing rule XML-03 gets one example (distinct ids for a split and its join). No rule added. v2.1 states six rules explicitly after a pilot run: the validator's errors in 165 first models (GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, documentation guidelines only) showed which rules of the specification and of its XML schema the generator broke. Only validator results were used, never a reference model. Each new rule carries its source_clause and pilot_evidence (number of failures it addresses). v2.0 note: v2.0 adds five rules identified by a systematic gap check of the catalogue against the full OMG PDF (formal/13-12-09): SUB-07, GW-09, EVT-11, EVT-12, EVT-13, LANE-04. Each carries its source clause. Cleanup: each v2.1 rule keeps only what the 76 earlier rules did not state; errors already covered by an earlier rule (unique ids XML-03, existing references FLOW-01/XML-03, parallel join of exclusive branches GW-05, lane of the owning process LANE-02, connected paths PROC-03) are not repeated. XML-06 corrected to match the schema exactly (no documentation in definitions; ioSpecification needs inputSet and outputSet).
